Panama Canal. An artificial waterway connecting the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans across the Isthmus of Panama, engineered and built by the United States between nineteen hundred and four and nineteen fourteen. It revolutionized global shipping by eliminating the need to circumnavigate South America and became one of the most strategically important infrastructure projects of the twentieth century, though its construction and American control sparked lasting geopolitical tensions in Latin America.

The canal was built under President Theodore Roosevelt's administration as a crown jewel of American imperialism and naval strategy. It opened in nineteen fourteen but was controlled by the United States until nineteen seventy-seven. The French attempted to build the canal under Ferdinand de Lesseps from eighteen eighty-one to eighteen eighty-nine but abandoned the project after massive casualties from disease and engineering failures. The United States obtained the right to build the canal by supporting Panama's independence from Colombia in nineteen hundred and three, then signed the Hay-Bunau-Varilla Treaty granting the United States a perpetual lease and control of the canal zone.

Construction was a monumental feat. The canal required locks, massive chambers that raise and lower ships, excavation of the Culebra Cut through the continental divide, and construction of Gatun Lake, an artificial lake created to enable ships to pass. The canal reduced travel time from Asia to the United States East Coast by roughly half, fundamentally altering global trade and naval deployment strategies. Both world wars demonstrated its strategic value.

Disease, yellow fever and malaria, killed thousands during construction until American engineers, led by Colonel William Gorgas, implemented sanitation reforms that broke the cycle of epidemics. The canal's construction displaced indigenous Panamanian populations and environmental degradation was severe. American control became a symbol of Yankee imperialism in Central America. It connects to Theodore Roosevelt, president who championed the canal as an achievement of American engineering and power, to the United States, which built and controlled the canal as a cornerstone of hemispheric dominance, to Spain, whose colonial holdings in the Caribbean made the canal strategically vital for competing powers, to Imperialism, which the canal embodied through American imperial ambitions and strategic control of key global choke points, and to World War Two, when the canal became critical to United States military logistics and Pacific theater operations.
